title: Two Addresses on the Camino Real del Oeste: the Engineer of the Lilies and the Catalan Dome
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Engineer Without a Birth Certificate

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the year that cannot be right
stops.date_confidence: the only birth year in any reachable source, printed unsourced in the running prose of the Spanish Wikipedia article on the Casa de los Lirios; it would make him seventy-two at his first known commission and one hundred and seven at death, and nothing corroborates it
stops.campa: One parenthesis carries the whole of his origin. The Spanish Wikipedia article on the Casa de los Lirios says the building was raised between 1903 and 1905 by the engineer Eduardo Rodríguez Ortega, 1831 to 1938, and cites nothing for the figures. No birth certificate, no parish register, no port manifest stands behind them. The same article calls him Argentine; Barriada.com.ar calls him a Spanish engineer. No third document has been located that would decide between the two, and none that would fix the lifespan either.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Casa de los Lirios' (raw wikitext, Descripción section)
suggested_refs: Mimi Böhm and Fabio Grementieri, Buenos Aires: Art Nouveau (2005), listed in the Wikipedia bibliography and not consulted here

stops.name: Berlin, the title of ingeniero civil
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source; the family places the studies in Berlin without a year, and this date is set only to precede the Buenos Aires work
stops.campa: His grandson and namesake, interviewed in 2021, supplies the one fact the family kept: the old man studied in Berlin and came home an ingeniero civil. Berlin in these decades teaches reinforced concrete as arithmetic, and hands iron spans and cement calculations to engineers rather than to artists. He takes the German title and not a French or a Catalan one. A century later the sources that reach for a professional word still call him ingeniero far more often than arquitecto.
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 'El Palacio de los Lirios, una perla del Art Nouveau en plena avenida Rivadavia', 10 February 2021, quoting the architect's grandson
suggested_refs: Enrolment registers of the Königlich Technische Hochschule zu Berlin, unsearched

stops.name: Charlottenburg, hizo muchas cosas
stops.date_confidence: wholly undocumented; the grandson says only that his grandfather did many things in Berlin and spent a long time in Europe, and the polytechnic is an inference from the period's usual route for foreign engineers
stops.campa: Asked what his grandfather actually built there, the grandson answers that he did many things, hizo muchas cosas, and stops. No German commission, drawing, employer or diploma has been traced to him. The Charlottenburg polytechnic that trained most of the city's foreign engineers has produced no record that anyone has yet gone and looked for. Whatever the long European stay contained, what survives of it is three words spoken by a descendant a century later, in an interview about a building.
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting the architect's grandson
suggested_refs: Any German professional register of the 1880s and 1890s bearing the name Rodríguez Ortega; none located

stops.name: Barcelona, the question the family cannot answer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the family attests a long stay in Europe but names no Spanish city and no year, and no source places him in Barcelona or in Spain at all
stops.campa: Somewhere in the European years the record leans south, because nothing else explains what he builds afterward. Antoni Gaudí is at work in the Eixample, and the ornament that will hang on Avenida Rivadavia belongs to that grammar and to no other. Did the two men meet? The grandson, asked directly, says he does not know. No source places Rodríguez Ortega in Barcelona, or in Spain at all. Spanish Wikipedia settles for a careful formula: he has been catalogued as an admirer of the architect Antonio Gaudí.
stops.quote: ha sido catalogado como un admirador del arquitecto Antonio Gaudí
stops.quote_source: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Casa de los Lirios'; the underlying cataloguing is not named in the article
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting the architect's grandson
suggested_refs: The Casa Batlló, built 1904 to 1906 in the Eixample
The Parc Güell dragon, whose iron copy he will set on a Buenos Aires corner

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the practice brought home
stops.date_confidence: inferred: no arrival record of any kind survives, and the year is set backward from his first known commission in 1903
stops.campa: He brings his practice to a city adding people faster than it can name architects. The researcher Rodolfo Liechtenstein counts some two hundred and twenty ornate houses raised here between the end of the century and the First World War, and calls it a record period for construction in quantity and in quality. Into that boom walks a man with a German degree and no client. Nothing is recorded of how he found the first one, or of where he lived while he looked.
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Rodolfo Liechtenstein
suggested_refs: Passenger lists of the Buenos Aires port for 1900 to 1903, unsearched

segments.name: Avenida Rivadavia, the Camino Real del Oeste

stops.name: Balvanera, where palaces do not go
stops.date_confidence: attested for the setting, from the researcher's description of the avenue in the year of the commission
stops.campa: The fashionable circuit runs north, toward the Recoleta and Avenida Alvear. Avenida Rivadavia is still spoken of as the Camino real del Oeste, the road out of town, and Liechtenstein notes that the growth of Buenos Aires is bending precisely this way. A frontage in Balvanera costs what a narrow lot costs further north, and the buyer of one is not buying an address. The barrio is filling with apartment blocks and with Italian-trained builders working the Liberty line that comes out of Milan.
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Rodolfo Liechtenstein
suggested_refs: The barrio of Balvanera and its Liberty-style apartment architecture of the 1900s

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2027, the ground Capurro bought
stops.date_confidence: attested; both La Nación and Spanish Wikipedia date the start of construction to 1903
stops.campa: Miguel Capurro made his money in textiles and in wine. He buys the frontage at Rivadavia 2027 to 2031 and hires the engineer with the German degree. The commission is not a palace for a family to inhabit; it is a rental building that has to earn its keep, and everything extravagant about it will be paid for out of shop rents. Rodolfo Liechtenstein, the architecture researcher who has read the street, describes the client without affection: a millionaire who did not invest in education, but did invest in bricks.
stops.quote: un millonario que no invertía en educación, pero sí en ladrillos
stops.quote_source: Rodolfo Liechtenstein on Miguel Capurro, quoted in La Nación, 10 February 2021
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Rodolfo Liechtenstein
suggested_refs: Municipal building permits of the Ciudad de Buenos Aires for Av. Rivadavia 2027/2031, not consulted

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the plan and its two versions
stops.date_confidence: the plan is undated; this falls inside the documented 1903 to 1905 construction period
stops.campa: Commerce at the pavement, two shops flanking a central door for the residents, and floors of paired apartments above: both surviving descriptions agree that far, and both describe an income-producing machine with ornament across its entire face. They differ about the top. La Nación reports the third floor held back for the owning family. Spanish Wikipedia counts three upper floors of two apartments each and mentions no family floor at all. Who was meant to live under the cornice is settled by neither, and no plan or permit survives.
suggested_refs: The original plans of the Casa de los Lirios, not located in any archive reached

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the piedra París goes on
stops.date_confidence: undated within the 1903 to 1905 construction period
stops.campa: The face of the building is clad in what the trade calls piedra París, a manufactured stone imported to stand in for the solid European article. Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana, president of the city's Art Nouveau association, calls it a copy of the solid stone that was used in Europe. It arrives by ship, sets hard and takes carving as deeply as the quarried kind, which is the whole point of buying it. The sculptors cut into it directly, and the soot of the busiest street in the city has been settling into those cuts for a hundred and twenty years.
stops.quote: una copia de la piedra sólida que se usaba en Europa
stops.quote_source: Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana, Presidente de la Asociación Art Nouveau de Buenos Aires, quoted in La Nación, 10 February 2021
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana
suggested_refs: The trade in imported artificial stone for Buenos Aires facades, 1890 to 1914

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the Italian blacksmiths and the four-metre door
stops.date_confidence: undated within the construction period; La Nación names the craftsmen without a year
stops.campa: The railings of every balcony and the ornament of the entrance door are wrought by blacksmiths who came from Italy. The engineer trained in Berlin forges none of it himself; he draws the line and hands it to men who crossed the Atlantic to hammer flowers out of a metal that has to be heated twice for every curve. No workshop is named in any source, and no smith. The door stands about four metres high, its iron drawn into iris leaves that bend as though under their own weight, and it is the piece visitors still stop at first.
stops.quote: las barandas de los balcones y la decoración de la puerta - todas de hierro - fueron hechas por herreros que venían de Italia
stops.quote_source: Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana, quoted in La Nación, 10 February 2021
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana
suggested_refs: The Italian immigrant ironworking trade of Buenos Aires in the 1900s; no workshop is named in any source

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the irises and the hyacinths
stops.date_confidence: undated within the construction period
stops.campa: Sculptors cut the flowers into the stone. Lirios run across the front, and bunches of jacinto encircle the whole width beneath the capital. The building takes its name from the first of them and keeps it: Casa de los Lirios, the house of the lilies, although what the ironwork actually draws is the iris. No sculptor is named in any source and no contract has surfaced. The orchids that later descriptions add are carved on no wall of the building and appear in no document about it.
suggested_refs: The sculptors of the Rivadavia 2031 relief, unidentified in every source consulted

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the wall that appears to move
stops.date_confidence: undated; placed at the completion of the facade
stops.campa: Bow windows push out of the wall and draw back into it. The string courses run in curves rather than in lines. In a street of flat Italianate fronts it is the one front for several blocks that behaves less like masonry than like something grown. Rodolfo Liechtenstein, architect and researcher, puts that in a sentence that has been quoted ever since: the facade is organic, which means that it takes its inspiration from nature, from movement and from undulation.
stops.quote: la fachada es orgánica, lo que significa que tiene su inspiración en la naturaleza, el movimiento y las ondulaciones
stops.quote_source: Rodolfo Liechtenstein, quoted in La Nación, 10 February 2021, and in Spanish Wikipedia, 'Casa de los Lirios'
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Rodolfo Liechtenstein
suggested_refs: Rodolfo Liechtenstein's Arquiviajes Buenos Aires walking itineraries of the Art Nouveau city

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the head at the cornice
stops.date_confidence: undated; placed at the completion of the cornice, in the final year of construction
stops.campa: At the centre of the cornice a plaster head of an old man looks down the avenue, his hair and beard running out sideways to become the rooftop railing. Liechtenstein reads him as wind, freedom, the search for something new. Some accounts name him Aeolus, who keeps the winds in a bag; others name him Neptune, who has no business this far from any water. Aeolus or Neptune? Nothing on the building says, and no drawing or contract has surfaced. He has been looking west along Rivadavia since 1905.
stops.quote: representa el viento, la libertad, la búsqueda de algo nuevo
stops.quote_source: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Casa de los Lirios', on the plaster head; the phrase is unattributed within the article
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Rodolfo Liechtenstein
suggested_refs: The Aeolus and Neptune attributions of the cornice head, both current and neither sourced

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the building finished
stops.date_confidence: the year 1905 is attested by both La Nación and Spanish Wikipedia; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: The work that began in 1903 finishes in 1905. Capurro has his rental building: a shop line at the pavement, let apartments above, and the most elaborate front standing for several blocks in either direction along an avenue the rich have not yet decided is respectable. It is also the first construction anyone can attach to the engineer's name. Nothing is recorded of what he was paid, who worked under him, or what he did in the following year. The tenants move in above the shops.
suggested_refs: The Casa de los Lirios, Av. Rivadavia 2027/2031, Balvanera, standing

stops.name: Buenos Aires, algo superfluo
stops.date_confidence: the observation is a modern one, by Pastrana in 2021, about the attitudes of this period; the date locates the attitude, not a documented event
stops.campa: The educated upper class of Buenos Aires does not commission work like this. To them Art Nouveau is algo superfluo, something superfluous, a shopkeeper's taste. Capurro, textiles and wine, has put a four-metre iron door and a plaster head of the wind on a public avenue that the older money declined to build on. Pastrana notes that the clients who did commission this architecture were the commercial bourgeoisie, and that they did so partly a modo contestatario, as an answer back.
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana and Rodolfo Liechtenstein
suggested_refs: The Asociación Art Nouveau de Buenos Aires and its inventory of the city's Art Nouveau stock

stops.name: Rivadavia and Ayacucho, the second commission
stops.date_confidence: contradicted: two Spanish Wikipedia articles, 'Balvanera' and 'Avenida Rivadavia', date the corner building to 1907, while the architect's grandson dates the same building to 1914; no municipal permit has been produced and the conflict is unresolved
stops.campa: A few metres east of the lily house, where Ayacucho meets Rivadavia, he builds again. The second building drops the imported French gloss of the first and abandons the flower relief entirely; what goes up on this corner is Catalan, and it says so on the roof in Catalan, in writing. Two Spanish Wikipedia articles date it to 1907. His own grandson, speaking in 2021, dates it to 1914. Both cannot be true, and no municipal permit has been produced by anyone.
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting the architect's grandson
suggested_refs: Municipal building permits for the corner of Av. Rivadavia and Ayacucho, unconsulted and decisive

stops.name: Rivadavia and Ayacucho, five storeys on a rounded pier
stops.date_confidence: undated within the disputed construction year; the five storeys are attested without a date
stops.campa: Five floors is high for Balvanera in this decade, higher than the lily house next door. The corner takes its load on a rounded pier instead of a right angle, and nothing about the massing is German or belongs to the Italianate street it stands on. Spanish Wikipedia records the five storeys, dates the building to 1907, and calls him Arq. rather than Ing., the only source that does. Of the ornament beneath the dome the same article says that it bears the unmistakable stamp of the Catalan style.
stops.quote: Tiene cinco pisos y fue construido en 1907 por el Arq. Eduardo Rodríguez Ortega
suggested_refs: The corner building at Av. Rivadavia and Ayacucho, Balvanera, standing and unlisted

stops.name: Rivadavia and Ayacucho, the glazed dome
stops.date_confidence: undated; the dome is attested without a completion date
stops.campa: The corner is crowned with a cúpula vidriada, glass held in an iron frame, lit from within at night and visible several blocks along the avenue in either direction. Around its base runs a line of lettering. Domes on Buenos Aires corners are ordinary by 1907; this one is not masonry with a lantern but glass all the way round, and it is the highest point on the stretch. No engineer of record is credited with the ironwork that holds it up, and no source says who glazed it.
suggested_refs: Barriada.com.ar, 'No hay sueños imposibles' (2011), the underlying source, blocked to direct fetch

stops.name: Rivadavia and Ayacucho, the sentence on the roof
stops.date_confidence: undated; the inscription is transcribed by Spanish Wikipedia without a date of installation
stops.campa: The legend set into the dome reads No hi ha somnis impossibles. There are no impossible dreams. It is not Spanish and it is not Latin. It is Catalan, on a building in a Spanish-speaking city eleven thousand kilometres from anyone who would read it without effort. Who chose it, the client or the engineer, is recorded nowhere. Spanish Wikipedia transcribes the line from barriada.com.ar and a TripAdvisor listing, neither of which could be fetched directly here.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the glazed dome, Av. Rivadavia and Ayacucho, Buenos Aires; transcribed in Spanish Wikipedia, 'Balvanera'
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Balvanera', citing barriada.com.ar and a TripAdvisor listing
suggested_refs: The Catalan colony of Buenos Aires in the 1900s, unexamined in relation to this inscription

stops.name: Rivadavia and Ayacucho, the iron dragon
stops.date_confidence: undated; the ornament is attested without a date of installation
stops.campa: An iron dragon is worked into the building, a direct quotation of Gaudí, who never built in Argentina and never crossed the Atlantic. The Spanish Wikipedia article on Avenida Rivadavia says the corner pays homage to the Catalan with an iron dragon similar to the one at the Parc Güell. Tourist material instead names the dragon door of the Casa Batlló, being finished in Barcelona in these same years. The two attributions circulate side by side, and no source reached here adjudicates between them.
stops.quote: un dragón de hierro similar al del Parc Güell
stops.quote_source: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Avenida Rivadavia', on the corner building at Ayacucho
suggested_refs: The Parc Güell dragon, Barcelona
The dragon door of the Casa Batlló, the competing and unsourced attribution

stops.name: Rivadavia and Ayacucho, the family claim of the first concrete
stops.date_confidence: the grandson's date for the corner building, against 1907 in two Spanish Wikipedia articles; the reinforced-concrete claim itself rests on this single family testimony and is corroborated by no engineering-history source
stops.campa: The family claim is a large one: that this was the first building in Buenos Aires made with reinforced concrete, raised with a technology the engineer had carried back from Europe himself. It is reported by one journalist quoting one descendant, and no engineering history corroborates it. Barriada.com.ar meanwhile makes a competing first for the lily house, calling it among the earliest reinforced-concrete buildings in Argentina. That is two buildings a few metres apart, each claimed first by a different source. No history of Argentine construction was located that mentions either one.
stops.quote: la primera edificación de Buenos Aires hecha con hormigón armado
stops.quote_source: The architect's grandson, Eduardo Rodríguez Ortega, quoted in La Nación, 10 February 2021
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting the architect's grandson
suggested_refs: A history of reinforced concrete construction in Argentina, which would settle both claims and was not located

stops.name: Buenos Aires, no third building
stops.date_confidence: arbitrary within the empty decades; nothing whatever is documented for him between the corner building and 1938
stops.campa: After the corner at Ayacucho the record stops. No third building is attributed to him anywhere. No professional society lists him, no competition entry or municipal appointment carries his name, no office address survives, and there is no marriage certificate and no birthplace. He is a working engineer in a city building at a rate it will never match again, and for roughly a quarter of a century he leaves behind nothing that anyone has found. Whether he kept practising at all is a question the record does not answer.
sources: Compiled gap: Spanish Wikipedia ('Casa de los Lirios', 'Balvanera', 'Avenida Rivadavia'), La Nación (2021), Barriada.com.ar; no further source located
suggested_refs: Rolls of the Sociedad Central de Arquitectos and the Centro Nacional de Ingenieros, unsearched for his name

stops.name: Balvanera, the avenue thickens around the two buildings
stops.date_confidence: no event is documented here; the date marks the intervening period, in which nothing about him is recorded
stops.campa: The avenue fills in around his work. The barrio thickens with apartment blocks, Once beside it becomes the centre of Jewish Buenos Aires, and the trams give way to a subte running underneath Rivadavia. The lily house passes through tenants nobody has listed and shopfronts that change hands unrecorded. Of the man who built it there is nothing at all in these years. The plaster head keeps its position at the cornice, taking the soot of a street that now carries more traffic than any other in the country.
suggested_refs: The tenancy records of Av. Rivadavia 2027/2031, not located

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the apartment on the second floor
stops.date_confidence: the grandson dates the intended move to 1938; the source gives no month and no confirmation from any other record
stops.campa: In old age he decides to move into his own building. The apartment he wants is on the second floor of the lily house and it is occupied, so he waits for the tenants' lease to run out. He had drawn the front door, the iron irises and the head at the cornice, and the plan of that room as well. No source gives the number of the apartment, the name of anyone living in it, or how long he had been waiting. His grandson says only that his grandfather died before the tenants' contract expired.
stops.quote: mi abuelo murió antes de que a los inquilinos de entonces se les venciera el contrato
stops.quote_source: The architect's grandson, Eduardo Rodríguez Ortega, quoted in La Nación, 10 February 2021
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting the architect's grandson
suggested_refs: The second-floor apartments of the Casa de los Lirios, still let

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the year given everywhere
stops.date_confidence: single-source and family-adjacent: 1938 appears in an unsourced Wikipedia parenthesis, the same string whose birth year is demonstrably wrong, and in a family anecdote that places him alive in 1938 without stating the year of death; no obituary or civil record has been located, and the month here is arbitrary
stops.campa: The year given everywhere is 1938. It rests on two things: a parenthesis in a Wikipedia article that also asserts a birth in 1831, and a grandson's account of a move that never happened. Neither is a record of a death. The anecdote in fact says only that he died before a running lease expired, which is compatible with a later year. So the death of a man who put two buildings on the busiest avenue in Argentina is dated from a newspaper anecdote and an uncited parenthesis. No obituary, no burial register and no civil record has been produced by any search made here, and neither source names a month or a day.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Casa de los Lirios' (the parenthesis '(1831-1938)', unsourced)
La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting the architect's grandson
suggested_refs: Argentine civil death registers for 1938 and after, unsearched

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a grave nobody has found
stops.date_confidence: no burial place is named in any reachable source and no date of interment is recorded; the date follows the presumed death only for ordering
stops.campa: Where he is buried is not known. Neither Chacarita nor Recoleta nor any parish register has been searched to a result in any source that can be reached, and no monument, plaque or headstone bearing his name has been reported anywhere in the city. Neither of the two buildings on Rivadavia carries his name on the outside. The burial registers of the Chacarita, the obvious place to begin, have not been searched by anyone whose result can be read. His grandson, who supplied the only biography anyone has, is not recorded as naming a cemetery either.
sources: Compiled gap: no cemetery, tomb, or burial record located in any accessible source
suggested_refs: The burial registers of the Cementerio de la Chacarita, unsearched

stops.name: Plaza del Congreso, expediente 2993/06
stops.date_confidence: the expediente number fixes the year 2006; the day and month of filing are not given in the archived listing reached
stops.campa: Senator Luis A. Falcó files expediente 2993/06 in the Argentine Senate, proposing that the Palacio de los Lirios be declared a Monumento Histórico Nacional. The Congress stands four blocks east of it along the same avenue. What became of the bill afterward is not recorded in any source reached here. A century after the shops opened, a rental block commissioned by a wine merchant and designed by an engineer with no biography has gone before the national legislature under the word monumento.
sources: Senado de la Nación Argentina, expediente PL 2993/06 (Sen. Luis A. Falcó), archived listing linked from Spanish Wikipedia, 'Casa de los Lirios'
suggested_refs: The full text and legislative fate of expediente PL 2993/06, unretrieved

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, listed Representativo
stops.date_confidence: the year of the catalogue listing is given by no source whatever; this date is a placeholder inside the period during which the protection is known to be in force
stops.campa: The Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires classes the Casa de los Lirios as Representativo and gives it nivel integral de protección, the comprehensive tier, covering facade and structure together. The corner building a few metres east at Ayacucho, with its glass dome and its iron dragon, carries no protection tier at all in any article that mentions it: one of the two is defended by law and the other is not. No source gives the year the listing was enacted, and the catalogue entry itself has not been retrieved.
stops.quote: cuenta con un nivel integral de protección
stops.quote_source: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Casa de los Lirios', on the city heritage catalogue
suggested_refs: The Catálogo de Inmuebles Patrimoniales of the Ciudad de Buenos Aires, for the year of listing

stops.name: Av. Rivadavia 2031, the journalist finds the grandson
stops.date_confidence: attested; the article is dated 10 February 2021
stops.campa: Germán Wille publishes a profile of the building in La Nación and does the one thing no researcher had done: he finds the grandson. Eduardo Rodríguez Ortega, named for the engineer, supplies Berlin, the long stay in Europe, the uncertainty about Gaudí and the apartment never occupied. The fullest account of the man's life anyone has assembled runs to one newspaper article, and this is it. Pastrana, quoted in the same piece, calls the building a jewel of elegance, of refinement and of the expression of nature.
stops.quote: Este edificio es realmente una joya de la elegancia, del refinamiento y de la expresión de la naturaleza.
stops.quote_source: Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana, Presidente de la Asociación Art Nouveau de Buenos Aires, quoted in La Nación, 10 February 2021
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 'El Palacio de los Lirios, una perla del Art Nouveau en plena avenida Rivadavia', 10 February 2021
suggested_refs: Mimi Böhm and Fabio Grementieri, Buenos Aires: Art Nouveau (2005), the one print monograph named and not consulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the American capital of Art Nouveau
stops.date_confidence: attested; the counts are Pastrana's, given in the article of 10 February 2021
stops.campa: Pastrana counts roughly three hundred buildings with Art Nouveau characteristics standing in Buenos Aires, seventy-five of them of high architectural quality, and on that count calls the city the American capital of Art Nouveau. Liechtenstein puts the wider boom at some two hundred and twenty ornate houses raised between the end of the nineteenth century and the First World War, a record period for construction in quantity and in quality. Two of them are Rodríguez Ortega's.
sources: La Nación, Germán Wille, 10 February 2021, quoting Juan Carlos Willy Pastrana and Rodolfo Liechtenstein
suggested_refs: The Asociación Art Nouveau de Buenos Aires inventory of some three hundred buildings

stops.name: Rivadavia and Ayacucho, the dome still lit
stops.date_confidence: present state, as described in the sources of 2021
stops.campa: The dome is still there, glass and iron above the intersection, its Catalan sentence running round the base while the buses stop underneath. Nobody in the queue reads Catalan. The building has no plaque, no protection tier and no agreed construction date; the man who raised it has no birth year, no birthplace, no third commission and no grave. What he has is a line on a roof, in a language nobody down here speaks, saying that there are no impossible dreams.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the glazed dome, Av. Rivadavia and Ayacucho, Buenos Aires
suggested_refs: The corner building at Av. Rivadavia and Ayacucho, unprotected and undated
